{{Short description|Mathematical conjectures in class field theory}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''local Langlands conjectures''', introduced by [[Robert Langlands]],{{sfnp|Langlands|1967}}{{sfnp|Langlands|1970}} are part of the [[Langlands program]]. They describe a correspondence between the [[complex number|complex]] [[group representation|representations]] of a [[reductive group|reductive]] [[algebraic group]] <math>G</math> over a [[local field]] <math>F</math>, and representations of the [[Langlands group]] of <math>F</math> into the <math>L</math>-group of <math>G</math>. This correspondence is not a [[bijection]] in general. The [[conjecture]]s can be thought of as a generalization of [[local class field theory]] from [[abelian group|abelian]] [[Galois group]]s to non-abelian Galois groups.

==Local Langlands conjectures for GL<sub>1</sub>==

The local Langlands conjectures for <math>\operatorname{GL}_1(K)</math> follow from (and are essentially equivalent to) [[local class field theory]]. More precisely, the [[Artin map]] gives an [[isomorphism]] from the group  <math>\operatorname{GL}_1(K)=K^\times</math> to the [[abelianization]] of the [[Weil group]]. In particular, [[irreducible representation|irreducible]] smooth representations of <math>\operatorname{GL}_1(K)</math> are {{nowrap|1-dimensional}} as the group is abelian, so can be identified with [[homomorphism]]s of the Weil group to <math>\operatorname{GL}_1(\C)</math>. This gives the Langlands correspondence between  homomorphisms of the Weil group to <math>\operatorname{GL}_1(\C)</math> and 
irreducible smooth representations of <math>\operatorname{GL}_1(K)</math>.

==Representations of the Weil group==

Representations of the Weil group do not quite correspond to irreducible smooth representations of [[general linear group]]s. To get a bijection, one has to slightly modify the notion of a representation of the Weil group, to something called a Weil–Deligne representation. This consists of a representation of the Weil group on a [[vector space]] <math>V</math> together with a [[nilpotent]] endomorphism <math>N</math> of <math>V</math> such that <math>wNw^{-1}=\|w\|N</math>, or equivalently a representation of the [[Weil–Deligne group]]. In addition, the representation of the Weil group should have an open kernel and be (Frobenius) semisimple.

For every Frobenius semisimple complex <math>n</math>-dimensional Weil–Deligne representation <math>\rho</math> of  the Weil group of <math>F</math> there is an [[L-function]] <math>L(s,\rho)</math> and a [[Langlands–Deligne local constant|local {{nowrap|ε-factor}}]] <math>\varepsilon(s,\rho,\psi)</math> (depending on a character <math>\psi</math> of <math>F</math>).

==Representations of GL<sub>''n''</sub>(''F'')==

The representations of <math>\operatorname{GL}_n(F)</math> appearing in the local Langlands correspondence are smooth irreducible complex representations. 
*"Smooth" means that every vector is fixed by some open subgroup.
*"Irreducible" means that the representation is nonzero and has no [[subrepresentation]]s other than 0 and itself.

Smooth irreducible complex representations are automatically admissible.

The [[Bernstein–Zelevinsky classification]] reduces the classification of irreducible smooth representations to cuspidal representations.

For every irreducible admissible complex representation <math>\pi</math> there is an ''L''-function <math>L(s,\pi)</math> and a local <math>\varepsilon</math>-factor <math>\varepsilon(s,\pi,\psi)</math> (depending on a character <math>\psi</math> of <math>F</math>). More generally, if there are two irreducible admissible representations <math>\pi</math> and <math>\pi'</math> of general linear groups, there are local Rankin–Selberg convolution L-functions <math>L(s,\pi\times \pi')</math> and <math>\varepsilon</math>-factors <math>\varepsilon(s,\pi\times \pi',\psi)</math>.

[[Colin Bushnell|Bushnell]] and [[Philip Kutzko|Kutzko]]{{sfnp|Bushnell|Kutzko|1993}} described the irreducible admissible representations of general linear groups over local fields.

==Local Langlands conjectures for GL<sub>2</sub>==

The local Langlands conjecture for <math>\operatorname{GL}_2</math> of a local field says that there is a (unique) bijection <math>\pi</math> from 2-dimensional semisimple Weil-Deligne representations of the Weil group to irreducible smooth representations of <math>\operatorname{GL}_2(F)</math> that preserves ''L''-functions, <math>\varepsilon</math>-factors, and commutes with twisting by characters of <math>F^\times</math>.

[[Hervé Jacquet|Jacquet]] and Langlands{{sfnp|Jacquet|Langlands|1970}} verified the local Langlands conjectures for <math>\operatorname{GL}_2</math> in the case when the residue field does not have [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] 2. In this case, the representations of the Weil group are all of cyclic or dihedral type. 

{{harvtxt|Gelfand|Graev|1962}} classified the smooth irreducible representations of <math>\operatorname{GL}_2(F)</math> when <math>F</math> has odd residue characteristic (see also {{harv|Gelfand|Graev|Pyatetskii-Shapiro|1969|loc=chapter 2}}), and claimed incorrectly that the classification for even residue characteristic differs only insignifictanly from the odd residue characteristic case. 
[[André Weil|Weil]]{{sfnp|Weil|1974}} pointed out that when the residue field has characteristic 2, there are some extra exceptional 2-dimensional representations of the Weil group whose image in <math>\operatorname{PGL}_2(\C)</math> is of tetrahedral or octahedral type. (For global Langlands conjectures, 2-dimensional representations can also be of icosahedral type, but this cannot happen in the local case as the Galois groups are [[solvable group|solvable]].)

[[Jerrold B. Tunnell|Tunnell]]{{sfnp|Tunnell|1978}} proved the local Langlands conjectures for the general linear group <math>\operatorname{GL}_2(K)</math> over the [[p-adic number|2-adic numbers]], and over local fields containing a [[cube root of unity]]. Kutzko{{sfnp|Kutzko|1980}} proved the local Langlands conjectures for the general linear group <math>\operatorname{GL}_2(K)</math> over all local fields.

[[Pierre Cartier (mathematician)|Cartier]],{{sfnp|Cartier|1981}} as well as Bushnell and [[Guy Henniart|Henniart]],{{sfnp|Bushnell|Henniart|2006}} gave  expositions of the proof.

==Local Langlands conjectures for GL<sub>''n''</sub>==<!-- [[Harris–Taylor]] redirects here -->

The local Langlands conjectures for general linear groups state that there are unique bijections <math>\pi\leftrightarrow \rho_\pi</math> from [[equivalence class]]es of irreducible admissible representations <math>\pi</math> of <math>\operatorname{GL}_n(F)</math> to equivalence classes of continuous Frobenius semisimple complex <math>n</math>-dimensional Weil–Deligne representations <math>\rho_\pi</math> of  the Weil group of <math>F</math> that preserve ''L''-functions and <math>\varepsilon</math>-factors of pairs of representations, and coincide with the Artin map for {{nowrap|1-dimensional}} representations. In other words,
* <math>L(s,\rho_\pi\otimes \rho_{\pi'}) = L(s,\pi\times \pi')</math>
* <math>\varepsilon(s,\rho_\pi\otimes \rho_{\pi'},\psi) = \varepsilon(s,\pi\times \pi',\psi).</math>

[[Gérard Laumon|Laumon]], [[Michael Rapoport|Rapoport]] and [[Ulrich Stuhler|Stuhler]]{{sfnp|Laumon|Rapoport|Stuhler|1993}} proved the local Langlands conjectures  for the general linear group <math>\operatorname{GL}_n(K)</math> for positive characteristic local fields <math>K</math>. Carayol{{sfnp|Carayol|1992}} gave an exposition of their work.

[[Michael Harris (mathematician)|Harris]] and [[Richard Taylor (mathematician)|Taylor]]{{sfnp|Harris|Taylor|2001}} proved the local Langlands conjectures  for the general linear group <math>\operatorname{GL}_n(K)</math> for characteristic 0 local fields <math>K</math>. Henniart{{sfnp|Henniart|2000}} gave another proof. Carayol{{sfnp|Carayol|2000}} and Wedhorn{{sfnp|Wedhorn|2008}} gave expositions of their work.

==Local Langlands conjectures for other groups==

[[Armand Borel|Borel]]{{sfnp|Borel|1979}} and [[David Vogan|Vogan]]{{sfnp|Vogan|1993}} discuss the Langlands conjectures for more general groups. The Langlands conjectures for arbitrary reductive groups <math>G</math> are more complicated to state than the ones for general linear groups, and it is unclear what the best way of stating them should be. Roughly speaking, admissible representations of a reductive group are grouped into disjoint finite sets called ''L''-packets, which should correspond to some classes of homomorphisms, called ''L''-parameters, from the [[local Langlands group]] to the [[Langlands dual|''L''-group]] of <math>G</math>. Some earlier versions used the Weil−Deligne group or the Weil group instead of the local Langlands group, which gives a slightly weaker form of the conjecture. 
 
Langlands{{sfnp|Langlands|1989}} proved the Langlands conjectures for groups over <math>\R</math> and <math>\C</math> by giving the [[Langlands classification]] of their irreducible admissible representations (up to infinitesimal equivalence), or, equivalently, of their irreducible [[(g,K)-module|<math>(\mathfrak{g},K)</math>-modules]].

[[Gan Wee Teck|Gan]] and Takeda{{sfnp|Gan|Takeda|2011}} proved the local Langlands conjectures for the [[symplectic similitude group]] <math>\operatorname{GSp}(4)</math> and used that to deduce it for the [[symplectic group]] <math>\operatorname{Sp}(4)</math>.{{sfnp|Gan|Takeda|2010}}
